overview.text: Voting is the formal expression of a choice—usually on a ballot, though sometimes by voice or show of hands—used to select public officials or express a preference on a political question. In representative government, voters choose officials to make decisions on their behalf; voting can also register choices among courses of action. Its distinguishing feature is that individual choices are counted under an electoral system, whose rules determine how votes translate into winners or legislative seats. Some ballots ask for a single choice, while preferential systems let voters rank candidates. In the United States, ballots may be cast in person, early, or by mail, depending on state rules; procedures are designed to keep choices private.

key_facts.text: A vote formally indicates a choice between candidates or courses of action; it may be expressed on a ballot, by hand, or by voice.
In representative government, elections let people convey authority to officials who make decisions on their behalf.
Electoral systems differ in what voters mark—such as a candidate, a party, or ranked preferences—and in how votes are translated into winners or seats.
In an alternative-vote system, voters rank candidates; if no one wins a majority of first preferences, lower-ranked candidates are eliminated and votes are reassigned according to later preferences.
In the United States, in-person Election Day, early in-person, and mail voting are options, but procedures vary by state; election officials keep voters’ choices private.
